name: API Versioning
intent: Change an API without breaking the clients that already depend on it, by adding new behaviour alongside the old and retiring the old on a schedule.
scenario: The users API returns a single 'name' field. Product wants first and last name as separate fields. A mobile app that half the customers still run, and a partner integration, both read 'name'.
problem: You control the server but not the clients. Mobile apps stay installed for years, and partners update on their own schedule. Changing a response in place breaks everyone who relied on the old shape, and you cannot upgrade them all at once.

howItWorks.title: Know what counts as a breaking change
howItWorks.text: Removing or renaming a field, changing its type or meaning, making an optional input required, or changing an error code can break clients. Adding an optional field, a new endpoint or a new enum value that clients can ignore is usually safe, provided clients are written to ignore what they do not know.

howItWorks.title: Prefer additive changes
howItWorks.text: The cheapest versioning is none: add 'firstName' and 'lastName' and keep 'name' working. Mark the old field deprecated, tell users, and remove it later. Most changes can be made this way, which avoids maintaining parallel versions.

howItWorks.title: When you must break, publish a new version
howItWorks.text: Put the version in the URL (/v1/users, /v2/users), in a header, or in the media type. URL versions are the easiest to see, route and cache. The old version keeps running unchanged while clients migrate.

howItWorks.title: Deprecate with a schedule
howItWorks.text: Announce the date, add Deprecation and Sunset headers to old responses, measure which clients still call the old version, and contact them. Retire a version only when its traffic is gone or the deadline you promised has passed.

howItWorks.title: Keep the cost of old versions low
howItWorks.text: Run versions from one codebase, translating old requests into the new internal model at the edge, so a fix lands once. Limit how many versions are supported at a time, because each one has to be tested, secured and kept running.

pros: Existing clients keep working while the API evolves
Lets you fix design mistakes without a flag day
A published sunset date gives clients time to plan
Additive changes need no new version at all
cons: Every live version is more code, tests and operations
Clients can stay on old versions for years
Version sprawl confuses documentation and support
Translating between versions can hide subtle bugs
whenToUse: Public APIs and mobile apps, where you cannot force clients to upgrade
Any change that removes, renames or re-types something clients use
Partner integrations with their own release cycles
whenNotToUse: A private API where one team deploys the server and all clients together
Changes that are purely additive, where a new version is unnecessary
pitfalls: Changing the meaning of a field without changing its name
Clients that crash on unknown fields, which makes every addition breaking
Never retiring old versions, so you support five at once
Retiring a version without measuring who still uses it
